name: Kryz
confidence_why: Authier's 2009 reference grammar of the Alik dialect states repeatedly that nouns carry final accent while independent verbs and locative adverbs carry initial accent, and Borise's 2018 survey agrees that stress is set by part of speech, differing only in paraphrasing nominal stress as second-syllable rather than final for longer words.

catalog_quote: Les syllabes non accentuées sont prononcées nettement, sans altération des voyelles. L’accent est mélodique, montant ou descendant, et mériterait plus de recherches. Il n’y a en tout cas pas de tons absolus. Les adjectifs et participes épithètes ainsi que les génitifs sont proclitiques. Les noms sont accentués sur la syllabe finale; quelques suffixes nominaux sont accentués, ainsi les marques de pluriel -mi/-bi et -ar. Comme les formes verbales indépendantes, les adverbes de lieu ont un accent initial, avec un allongement expressif de la première syllabe. La place de l’accent permet de repérer la catégorie du mot, et distingue des formes segmentalement identiques. Les formes dépendantes ‘nominalisées’ du verbe (masdars, gérondifs et converbes, participes substantivés) ont l’accent final alors que les formes verbales indépendantes sont accentuées sur l’initiale; on a ainsi des paires minimales: yi-qr-íc ‘saisir’/ yí-qr-ic ‘a été saisi’; b-ar-í ‘faits / qui les a faits’/ b-ár-i ‘qu’on les fasse’.

Il n'y a en tout cas pas de tons absolus. Les adjectifs et participes épithètes ainsi que les génitifs sont proclitiques. Les noms sont accentués sur la syllabe finale ; quelques suffixes nominaux sont accentués, ainsi les marques de pluriel -mi/-bi et -ar. new_statements.translation: Unaccented syllables are pronounced clearly, without vowel alteration. The accent is melodic, rising or falling, and would merit more research. In any case there are no absolute tones. Attributive adjectives and participles as well as genitives are proclitic. Nouns are accented on the final syllable; some nominal suffixes are accented, e.g. the plural markers -mi/-bi and -ar. Like independent verb forms, adverbs of place have initial accent, with expressive lengthening of the first syllable. The place of the accent makes it possible to identify the word's category and distinguishes segmentally identical forms.
new_statements.citation: Authier, Gilles. 2009. Grammaire kryz (langue caucasique d'Azerbaïdjan, dialecte d'Alik). Collection Linguistique SLP 93. Leuven/Paris: Peeters. §2.8.2 'Accent de mot et parties du discours', p. 26.
new_statements.locator: printed p. 26, §2.8.2 (PDF page 30 of the uncorrected proofs); restated pp. 141 (§10.1), 143 (§10.1.4), 185 (§13.1)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (435 pp., text; source URLhttp://www.digitorient.com/wp/wp-content/uploads/2009/12/AUTHIERKryzGrammarUncorrectedproofs.pdfre-checked live today: HTTP 200, Content-Length 2287226 = copies we hold size). PDF page 30 = printed p. 26 carries the header "26 GRAMMAIRE KRYZ" and section "2.8.2. Accent de mot et parties du discours"; the quoted passage is there word for word (extracted text only differs by line-break hyphens: "procli-tiques"). The paragraph continues exactly as the compiler summarised: nominalised dependent verb forms (masdars, gerunds/converbs, substantivised participles) have final accent, independent verb forms initial accent, minimal pairs yi-qr-íc 'saisir' / yí-qr-ic 'a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-class-conditioned pitch accent: nouns and all nominalised/dependent verb forms (masdars, gerunds, converbs, substantivised participles, also the future built on the imperfective participle and the interrogative forms) carry the accent on the final syllable; independent finite verb forms (all indicative forms except the future) and place adverbs carry it on the initial syllable. Accent position distinguishes segmentally identical forms: yi-qr-íc 'to seize' (masdar) vs yí-qr-ic 'was seized' (aorist N); xhiyíc 'to become' vs xhíyic 'became'; b-ar-í 'done / who did them' vs b-ár-i 'let them be done'. The author describes the accent as melodic (pitch), rising or falling, and explicitly denies lexical tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; the negative future (a compound form) 'keeps two accents', that of the imperfective participle and of the independent negative copula (p. 150).
new_statements.exceptions: Future tense keeps the participle's final accent (p. 143); interrogative verb forms are final-accented (p. 144); nominal plural suffixes -mi/-bi and -ar attract the accent; adjectives, attributive participles and genitives are proclitic (unaccented); adjective loses its accent when attributive (p. ~350: 'tonique, et perd son accent s'il est épithète'); forms without final accent drop the pharyngeal of the locative -aˤ (p. 31). Borise 2018 (citing Saadiev 1994: 411) instead reports second-syllable stress on di- and trisyllabic nominals, which agrees with Authier only for disyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in the Alik dialect (Authier's data); at phrase level each constituent carries one pitch accent, on the last syllable of the nominal head base and the first syllable of the verb (p. 185). Author notes the accent is melodic and under-researched; no instrumental study.
new_statements.identity_note: Authier 2009 describes the Alik dialect (village of Alik/Əlik, Quba district; Khaput is very close to it) and states the finite verb forms differ considerably across the three dialects Kryz, Djek, Alik-Khaput; Glottolog lists no separate dialect glottocodes under kryt1240. Saadiev's sketches describe the Kryz-village dialect (and a now-extinct Ismayilli variety). Borise 2018's 'second syllable' for nominals (from Saadiev 1994: 411) vs Authier's 'final syllable' may reflect this dialect difference or a description difference; unresolved without Saadiev.

new_statements.translation: Unstressed syllables are pronounced clearly, without alteration of the vowels. The accent is melodic, rising or falling, and would deserve more research. In any case there are no absolute tones. Epithet adjectives and participles as well as genitives are proclitic. Nouns are accented on the final syllable; some nominal suffixes are accented, e.g. the plural markers -mi/-bi and -ar. Like independent verb forms, adverbs of place have initial accent, with expressive lengthening of the first syllable. The position of the accent makes it possible to identify the word's category and distinguishes segmentally identical forms. The dependent 'nominalised' forms of the verb (masdars, gerunds and converbs, substantivised participles) have final accent, whereas independent verb forms are accented on the initial; hence minimal pairs: yi-qr-íc 'to seize' / yí-qr-ic 'was seized'. [Also §13.1 p. 185: 'each constituent carries a pitch accent, on the last syllable of the bases of nominal heads, and on the first syllable of the verb.']

new_statements.relation_note: This is the very work behind the existing statement (Authier 2009 §2.8.2 p. 26); the quote matches the catalog's existing_statements verbatim and adds the §13.1 restatement ('accent de hauteur' on the last syllable of nominal heads and the first syllable of the verb). The catalog_records entry has an empty rule string, so this compilation fills it: category-determined edge accent (nominal final / finite verb initial), pitch-realised, no lexical tone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-class-determined edge accent, realised as pitch (melodic, rising or falling; no lexical tones): nominals (nouns, masdars, gerunds/converbs, substantivised participles, and the future formed on the imperfective participle, and interrogative verb forms) are accented on the final syllable, some plural suffixes (-mi/-bi, -ar) being accented; independent finite verb forms (all indicative forms except the future) and locative adverbs are accented on the initial syllable, with expressive lengthening of the first syllable in adverbs. Accent position is contrastive across categories (yi-qr-íc 'to seize' vs yí-qr-ic 'was seized'; b-ar-í vs b-ár-i). Epithet adjectives, epithet participles and genitives are proclitic (unaccented).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such. The compound negative future 'keeps two accents' (that of the imperfective participle and that of the independent negative copula), §10.6 p. 155: kurats'í dar.
new_statements.exceptions: Future tense retains final accent of the imperfective participle (§10.1.4 p. 143), unlike other indicative forms which are initial (§10.1 p. 141); interrogative verb forms are accented on the final (§10.2.1 p. 144); perfect and present negative forms have become initial because of an older cliticised copula while aorist and eventual negatives stay final like the non-finite forms (§10.6 p. 155); a participle heading an absolutive phrase is tonic but loses its accent when used as an epithet (§19.1.3); plural suffixes -mi/-bi and -ar attract accent; accent 'would deserve more research'.
new_statements.identity_note: Authier 2009 describes the Kryz dialect of Alik village (Quba district, NE Azerbaijan), stated on the title page and in §1.1; §10 notes that verbal forms differ across the three dialects (Kryz proper, Djek, Alik-Khaput) and that the description sticks to Alik usage. Glottolog kryt1240 covers Kryz as a whole, so the accent statement is strictly for the Alik dialect.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among works actually listed (only one open work, Authier 2009). One secondary-literature nuance held by the project but not in the 'works' list: Borise 2018 (ms., 'Word stress in the languages of the Caucasus', p. 10, citing Saadiev 1994: 411 and Authier 2009: 26, 141) paraphrases the nominal rule as 'di- and trisyllabic nominals.. are stressed on the second syllable', whereas Authier states 'les noms sont accentués sur la syllabe finale'. For disyllables these coincide; for trisyllabic nouns they would differ (second vs final). Saadiev 1994 (print only) could not be opened, so whether the 'second syllable' formulation is Saadiev's or Borise's simplification is unverified. Authier is the primary description of the Alik dialect and is the reading of record.

sources.note: p.10 (§5.2): 'stress placement varies by part of speech in Kryz. In Kryz, di- and trisyllabic nominals, including deverbal nominals such as masdars, are stressed on the second syllable, while most verbs (apart from future forms) and adverbs have initial stress. This leads to minimal pairs: jiqhríd͡ʒ 'grab.INF', jíqhrid͡ʒ 'grab.PST.PTCP' (Saadiev 1994: 411; Authier 2009: 26, 141).' Secondary; note 'second syllable' (attributed to Saadiev) vs Authier's 'final syllable' for nouns.

sources.note: In the Daghestanian section (based on his 1999 survey, ref. [9]) Kodzasov contrasts the Lezgian languages with initial-window stress (Lezgian, Agul, Rutul, Archi) and final-oriented Tabasaran with Tsakhur, where stress never became a general word property, and states that Budukh and Kryz have no stress at all and probably have syllabic tones, their word prosody needing further study. This first-hand phonetician's assessment differs from the on-file coding (Authier 2009: melodic word accent placed by word class, 'pas de tons absolus').

tone.quote: Акценты. По-видимому, большинство дагестанских языков имеет слоговой тональный акцент. Из обследованных нами языков такую систему имеют: все андийские и цезские, цахурский, будухский и крызский. Возможно, к этому же типу принадлежат лакский и удинский. ... СЛОГ И ПРОСОДИЯ ... 3. Словесного ударения нет. Размещение фразового акцента внутри слова не исследовано. Вероятно наличие слогового тона.

tone.translation: Accents. Apparently most Daghestanian languages have a syllabic tonal accent. Of the languages we surveyed, the following have such a system: all Andic and Tsezic, Tsakhur, Budukh and Kryz. Possibly Lak and Udi belong to the same type. ... SYLLABLE AND PROSODY ... 3. There is no word stress. The placement of phrasal accent within the word has not been investigated. The presence of syllable tone is probable.

A dissertation-length structural description of Kryz based mainly on the plain-village Kryz dialect with comparisons across dialects (Authier 2009: 4-5, who adds that Saadiev's notation is phonetic); Saadiev's derived 1994 sketch gives stress placement by part of speech (Saadiev 1994: 411 per Borise 2018), so the phonetics part of the dissertation is the likely fuller source of that account. No indication of any tone claim.
